equivocal

/ih-KWIV-uh-kul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Equivocal means deliberately ambiguous or vague, especially in wording chosen to avoid committing to a clear position.

When shareholders demanded a yes or no on the buyout, the chairman gave an equivocal reply that left both sides guessing.

Example

During a live interview, a tech executive was asked whether her company would cut jobs after the merger. She answered that the company 'always evaluates every option to serve our teams best.' Reporters replayed the clip for days, some hearing a promise of no layoffs, others hearing a warning of cuts to come. Her equivocal answer let listeners on both sides believe she agreed with them, which was exactly the point.

The executive's statement was deliberately worded so it could be read in opposite ways, letting her avoid committing to a clear position, which is what equivocal means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ambiguous: Ambiguous means open to more than one interpretation, and it carries no verdict about intent - a mumbled instruction or a badly placed comma can be ambiguous by pure accident. Equivocal adds calculation: the wording was chosen so it cannot be pinned down. Every equivocal answer is ambiguous, but only the deliberate ones are equivocal.

evasive: Evasive means deliberately avoiding a direct answer - dodging, changing the subject, pleading ignorance. An evasive speaker escapes the question; an equivocal one answers it, in words engineered to face both directions at once. Evasion leaves you with no answer; equivocation leaves you with two.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

unambiguous: having only one clear meaning

forthright: direct and plainspoken

Where it sits · how deceptive the wording is

noncommittal → equivocal → duplicitous

noncommittal vs. equivocal: A noncommittal answer simply declines to take a side, while an equivocal one is deliberately worded so it can be read more than one way.

duplicitous vs. equivocal: Equivocal language leaves a speaker's real position unclear, but duplicitous speech goes further, actively saying one thing while intending another.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — equi-: from Latin aequus, equal

Root — voc: from Latin vox and vocare, voice or to call

Suffix — -al: characteristic of, pertaining to

Put it together: Equivocal is built from equi- (equal) plus the Latin root voc (voice), literally 'of equal voice.' An equivocal answer speaks with equal voice on both sides of a question so no one can tell where the speaker stands. The suffix -al, meaning 'characteristic of or pertaining to,' turns that idea into an adjective describing statements that have the nature of this two-sided speech.

Use the root in a new word: equivocate: Rather than admit the project was late, the manager equivocated, literally speaking with 'equal voice' on both sides of the question.

Word Building

Word Choice

formal, often critical register

Equivocal typically describes answers, statements, responses, and results (an equivocal answer, equivocal test results). It describes the wording itself, not the person, and it usually implies the vagueness is deliberate; something merely unclear by accident is better called ambiguous.
